segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple, the one Jesus loved, and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have put him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter and the other disciple set out and were going to the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The two were running together, but the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and reached the tomb first.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Bending down to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Simon Peter also came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up in a place by itself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they did not yet understand the Scripture that he must rise from the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples went back home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Mary stood outside by the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had been lying, one at the head and one at the feet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to her,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Woman, why are you weeping?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have put him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, if you have carried him off, tell me where you have put him, and I will take him away.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Mary.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She turned and said to him in Hebrew,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbouni!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (which means Teacher).

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have seen the Lord,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that he had said these things to her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were locked where the disciples were, for fear of the Jewish leaders, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Peace be with you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to them again,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, I also am sending you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he breathed on them and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Receive the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven them; if you retain anyone’s, they are retained.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Thomas, one of the Twelve, who was called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the other disciples kept telling him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have seen the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger into the mark of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will never believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Eight days later his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Peace be with you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to Thomas,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Bring your finger here and look at my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side. Do not be unbelieving, but believing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thomas answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My Lord and my God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Because you have seen me, have you believed? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.

notes.note: In Greek this was an ordinary, courteous way to address a woman, with none of the abruptness that “Woman” has in modern English. Jesus uses the same address to his mother in this Gospel. The traditional word is kept because English has no natural equivalent; “Madam” and “Dear woman” each add a tone the Greek lacks.

The Greek word means “in the language of the Hebrews” and in this period could cover Aramaic as well as Hebrew proper. “Rabbouni” is usually identified as an Aramaic form, which is why some translations read “in Aramaic” here. In the Greek, Jesus also addresses Mary by the Semitic form of her name, Mariam.

notes.phrase: Do not hold on to me
notes.note: The older rendering “Touch me not” suggests that Jesus forbids any contact. The Greek is a present-tense prohibition, which commonly means “stop doing” something already under way, and the verb can mean to take hold of or cling to. Most modern scholars and translations therefore understand Jesus to be telling Mary to let go of him, though the exact force of the reason he gives is still debated.

The Greek says simply “the Jews,” the traditional rendering. The disciples behind the locked doors were themselves Jews, so the group they feared is the Jerusalem authorities who had just had Jesus put to death, and the translation makes that narrower reference explicit. Scholars are divided over how best to render this word in John; some prefer “Judeans,” others keep “Jews” throughout.

This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. It is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathes the breath of life into the first human (Genesis 2:7) and when breath enters the slain in Ezekiel’s vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). A reader who knew those passages would have heard an act of new creation. The Greek has no object, and “on them” is supplied for English.

Both “are forgiven” and “are retained” are perfect tenses in Greek, describing a settled state. Some interpreters press this to mean “they have already been forgiven,” so that the disciples announce what God has done; others take it simply as “they stand forgiven” once the disciples act. The grammar does not settle the question, and the rendering leaves it open.

Many translations leave the Greek word as a name, “Didymus.” It is the ordinary Greek word for a twin, and “Thomas” itself comes from the Aramaic word for twin, so John is giving his Greek readers the meaning of the name. The translation gives the meaning as some modern versions do. The text does not say whose twin he was.
Ancient counting normally included both the first and the last day. “Eight days later” therefore means a week later, on the following first day of the week, and some translations render it that way.

notes.traditional: Because you have seen me, you have believed.
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, so the sentence can be read as a question or as a statement (“Because you have seen me, you have believed”). The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used, which reads a question. The sense differs little either way: Thomas’s belief rests on sight, and the blessing is on those who believe without it.

The traditional rendering is “the Christ.” Here the word is a title with the article, the claim that Jesus is the anointed king Israel expected, and not a second name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels while keeping “Christ” where it works as a name.

Manuscripts differ by one letter between two forms of the verb. One form (followed here) most naturally suggests “go on believing”; the other could suggest “come to believe.” The difference bears on whether the Gospel was written mainly to strengthen believers or to win new ones, but scholars caution that the tense alone cannot decide this, and the evidence is closely balanced.

candidates.reason: Recurs in John, Acts and Revelation, and translators split between “in Hebrew” and “in Aramaic”; readers would be confused by variation across chapters.
The vocative address recurs across the Gospels (including to Jesus’s mother), and “Woman,” “Dear woman,” “Madam” or omission each give a different tone that should be uniform.
The vocative κύριε ranges from polite “Sir” to confessional “Lord,” and a consistent rule is needed for deciding which applies when the speaker’s understanding is unclear.
A key term in John and frequent elsewhere, where translations vary between “sign,” “miracle” and “miraculous sign.”
With sins as object, translators choose between “forgive,” “release” and “remit,” and the pairing with κρατέω (“retain”) here shows the choice affects wordplay across books.
